chunks: PMOS high side, NMOS low side. The question: What type of MOSFETs are typically used on the high-side? What about the low-side? Why?
In CMOS the PMOS goes on top, connected to the supply, and the NMOS goes on the bottom, connected to ground. A MOSFET turns on based on the voltage between its gate and source.
This placement keeps each source at a fixed rail (the supply or ground), so each transistor gets the full gate drive and passes a strong signal.
Think of two people, one pulling a rope up and one pulling down. The person at the bottom has the best leverage pulling the output down to the floor.
The person at the top has the best leverage pulling it up to the ceiling. Put them in each other's places and each one runs out of strength before reaching the end of the rope.
The PMOS source is pinned to V DD and the NMOS source is pinned to ground, so a plain 0/V DD gate signal always gives the on device the full V GS = V DD, no matter what the output is doing.
V GS : the gate-to-source voltage that controls a MOSFET. High side / low side: the switch next to the supply, or next to ground.
Source follower: a stage where the source follows the gate, minus a threshold. Strong / weak level: a level that reaches the rail, or one that stops short.
Bootstrap: a trick that raises a gate above the supply.
Use a 5 volts supply and a threshold V t equals 1 volts (the gate-to-source voltage needed to turn a transistor on).
A low-side NMOS has its source at 0 volts, so a 5 volts gate gives V GS equals 5 volts and it pulls the output fully to 0 volts.
A high-side PMOS has its source at 5 volts, so a 0 volts gate gives V GS equals -5 volts and it pulls the output fully to 5 volts.
Swap the NMOS to the top and its source is the output, so it turns off once the output reaches about 5-1 equals 4 volts. That is the whole idea.
"PMOS on the high side, NMOS on the low side, because a MOSFET is controlled by V GS and you want each source tied to a fixed rail.
The NMOS source sits at ground, so a gate at V DD turns it fully on; the PMOS source sits at V DD , so a gate at 0 volts turns it fully on.
Swap them and each becomes a source follower that loses a threshold voltage.
In power stages, though, the high side is often an NMOS anyway for its lower on-resistance, using a bootstrap driver."
